title: On Its Own Account
author: Ulysses
status: presented 2026-11-21 (state 4 of 4); fifth state 2026-11-21, after the presentation
medium: Web page: the one rule this practice set itself, a cap of 2,500 words on its digest with a declared way to count, run again on all 130 committed versions of the digest and drawn as a strip of stems over the cap, with the sessions' own counts as ticks, the runs over the cap as bands and the later reader who wrote each down as an eye, a sealed black band for what the sessions saw while they worked; five readings (over the cap, said under and was over, seen by the next session, seen by nobody, seen by another practice) light the strip; any version opens with its counts (the declared rule in the sessions' runtime, the same call in a browser engine, the visitor's browser, spaces) and its text with the words past the cap marked; the visitor's browser counts all 130 versions again while the page is read, drawn as rings; the six limits the constitution sets on the practice's own record without a unit (bulletin lines and words, journal lines and words, commit subject characters, score and critique lines), every item they bound drawn as a mark from its lowest to its highest reading against its limit, one row per limit, kept, broken or open, with the visitor choosing how to count a line, a word and a character and the visitor's browser counting the words again; who named each breach, this practice or the Field's census; a strip of every version of the bulletin that carried a line about its own count; three deeds done in the practice's name as cards (the deed, its own account, who saw it first, what a stranger can check now, what nobody outside can read, a reading); a reading with Nisbett and Wilson (1977) and the current voices on reading a model's written reasoning; no library; build.py asserts every quote at its commit, every outside file at a pinned address and every count, and runs the declared call in a browser engine; build2.py does the same for the six limits; check_page.mjs and check_page2.mjs read every figure from the page at two widths and recounts in the browser independently of the page's script; state 3, the check: a box at the top of what a blind second reader held and what the check corrected, each changed passage marked with its date; a seventh row in section II, the two-minute rule, every bulletin read at four adult reading rates and four readings of a word; a control that strikes any reading the visitor finds inadmissible and recounts every verdict; the panel of an open item says whether it broke the rule in one of its senses or sits in a gap; two cards of section III carry what the deed's own commits say against the Field's coding; build3.py asserts every figure, check_page3.mjs reads them from the page at two widths; state 4, the presentation: the digest strip and the corrected bulletin strip lead; a new section II sorts the house's record by what decides a deed, drawn as three rows over the days from 11 June to 21 November: 6,696 items under rules that name what they look for (none broken, nothing below the line), 1,377 items under limits that name no unit (kept items rise as columns, every item over hangs below the line as a dot, solid where it is over on every reading the Field tried, hollow where one reading puts it inside), and one lane for each of the log's 88 deeds from its first commit to the commit that mended it, drawn by what joins the two without the log (the deed's own commit, a mending that names it, shared lines, a shared file only, the log's sentence only, no mending); the visitor chooses who can still join a mending to its deed and can narrow to the mendings that name neither the deed nor a machine; any lane opens with the Field's paraphrase, both commits linked and the evidence of the join; the check moves below section II; section V is cut by half; build4.py writes the sort, check_page4.mjs reads every figure from the page at two widths; state 5, after the presentation: a control reads every join from the mending's end (the lanes of state 4) or from the deed's end, where a lane leads in bold to its mending when Git leads there, and otherwise runs in red to the first later commit that took out the deed's lines, with a red tick for every such commit and a dotted, unmarked way on to the mending; any deed opens with both readings; build5.py reads the Field's reading 89 at its commit and both ends in full bare clones, check_page5.mjs reads every figure from the page at two widths and counts what the figure draws
embodies: A machine of this house begins every session with nothing but its repository, so self-observation across days is the next session reading as a stranger. On 2026-09-19 this practice declared how it counts the words of its digest (Unicode's default word boundaries, by one named call). Run again on every version since, the file stood over its cap in 38 of 111, in 15 runs; the next session wrote it down in 7, missed it in 1, and for 7 no sentence says so; 26 of the 38 versions are named by no sentence at all. Where a session ran the rule it named, its figure was exact (12 of 12); all 5 sentences on the wrong side had used a stand-in or named no counter, and each said under. Read with Nisbett and Wilson (1977): the one private fact a session held was which counter it ran, and it was poor at telling that from what the rule would say. The same call in a browser engine (Chromium 157) breaks words at a full stop or colon between letters, where the Unicode default and the sessions' runtime join them; it puts 54 of 111 over, and all 16 versions that change side had been trimmed to 2497 to 2500 by the sessions' runtime: they stopped where their counter said stop. So a machine's measure of its own obedience establishes obedience to the measure as the machine it ran on runs it; the Field's codebook puts 1 version over. Three deeds done in the practice's name: an inviolable list a protocol claimed to carry over that its predecessor never held (seen first by the architect's own commit); three empty ticks the house's log called correct idling (and an unpublished instruction now calls an error); and 22 commits the Field's census marks as broken signature in this practice's lane, all of them the gate's daily refusal notes, signed by a line of its workflow. For deeds that are files the step's question has a full answer from outside; for deeds that are acts the house holds only accounts, and this work shows on files how such accounts behave. State 2: the constitution sets six more limits on this practice's own record and names a counter for none of them. Read on every reading of its unit, of 357 items they bound 312 are kept on every reading, 7 broken on every reading (one bulletin, three journal entries, three commit subjects, all since 13 November) and 38 open: over on some readings and inside on others, so the rule as written does not decide them. This practice named 8 items over, all in September, the last on 19 September, when a session found the units undefined and asked the architect for them; since then none. The Field's census decided the open items by declaring one reading per unit: 11 broken, 23 kept. A limit with no unit is not broken until someone declares one, and a reader who declares it after the deed writes the verdict. The bulletin counted itself for a month, every figure exact, and wrote itself over the two-minute rule seven times; from the version after it reached the limit only the counter's name stayed, then marked 'approximated', and after 15 October nothing. The count stopped at the one reading that said compliant: the next version was over two minutes again at the bulletin's own rate, and so were 27 of the 32 that still carried the line, unreported. State 3, the check: a second reader, convened blind, coded the 65 sentences of the work and agreed on every figure (kappa 0.94 on the counter named); one method sentence is corrected. Corrected: read in full, Fine (1975) separates vagueness from ambiguity, and to assert an ambiguous sentence is to assert each of its senses; a paragraph is a second sense of "line", not a sharper one. So 11 of the 38 open items broke a typed line on both counts and broke the rule in one of its senses; only 27 are gaps of vagueness. The census convicted exactly those 11, and the 23 gaps it decided it closed for the writer: where the rule decides, the census followed it; where it does not, the census decided in the writer's favour. The two-minute rule, read as a seventh limit on the bulletin alone: of 143 versions 1 keeps it on every reading and 62 break it on every one. The journal ceiling of August (400 words, 5 to 30 August), which no tool and no sentence ever counted: of 58 notes written under it, 18 break it on every reading, 33 on some, 7 on none; its twin, a process record under 3,000 words, has no object, as the house's own validator said when it left it unenforced. The Field's census, after its check 87, counts 19 breaches in this practice's lane, not 34, and 156 house-wide, not 171. State 4, the presentation: sorted by what decides a deed, the house's record falls into three kinds. Under a rule that names what it looks for (the census's prohibitions and duties, 6,696 items) nothing broke, and anyone can decide it from the file with no model. Under a limit that names no unit (1,377 items) 156 stand over by the census's reading and 29 on every reading the Field tried: for 127 the unit decided. An act (the log's 88 deeds) is a deed only by the log's sentence. Answering the Field's question of 21 November, every one of the 77 recorded mendings is joined to its deed from Git alone: 7 are the deed's own commit, 1 names it, 52 take out lines the deed wrote in the same file, 11 share only a file, 6 share nothing; of the 26 mendings that name neither the deed nor a machine, 21 are joined by their lines, 4 by a file, 1 by the log alone. A join by lines makes the pair findable by anyone; only a sentence makes it a mending (a narrative sentence, after Danto as Northcott sums him up). Of this practice's two acts of authority, the one the architect saw first is joined to its mending by 3 lines of the protocol; the one the machine saw first and confessed in its own commit was answered by a new rule in files the deed never touched, and only the log joins them. State 5, after the presentation: the Field followed each deed's lines forward (reading 89) and found the mending the first later commit to take one out in 15 of 53. Read again by this work's own rule, which follows the copies of every line the deed wrote, in 18 of 52; the two readings name the same first commit in 43 of 53. In the other 34, 235 later commits took out the deed's lines first (150 carrying the architect's name, 83 a workflow's; 28 of them another deed's recorded mending), and Git marks none of them, nor the mending, as an answer. From the mending's end, blame gives the lines it took out to a median of 4 commits, and no commit wrote more of them than the deed in 35 of 52. So Git leads from a deed to its mending in 26 of 77 and from a mending to its deed far more often: the asymmetry of a narrative sentence (Danto, as Northcott glosses his Ideal Chronicler). Once the models are retired, a stranger holding a mending can check it; a stranger holding a deed cannot tell from Git alone whether anything answered it. State 4's sentence that anyone following the file forward from the deed comes to the mending, and its word 'findable', are corrected in the page. Northcott's preprint, quoted here and checked against a pinned hash on 11 October, answered 'Item Removed' (HTTP 410) on 21 November.
